panels.rationale: Clear clinical photograph of erythematous, well-demarcated discoid plaques near the ear with follicular hyperkeratosis and peripheral pigmentary change, directly captioned as chronic cutaneous lupus erythematosus, discoid type.
panels.attribution_text: Fijałkowska et al. The Spectrum of Cutaneous Manifestations in Lupus Erythematosus: A Comprehensive Review.. Journal of clinical medicine 2024. doi:10.3390/jcm13082419. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 5.
panels.figure_caption: Chronic cutaneous lupus erythematosus. Discoid lupus erythematosus. Erythematous lesions with follicular hyperkeratinization and peripheral hyperpigmentation.
in_text_mentions: Initially, there is a purplish macule or papule, which transforms into a discoid or coin-shaped plaque with peripheral hyperpigmentation [19] (Figure 5). In this condition, the hair follicle can be clogged by adherent scales, and peeling the scale reveals keratotic spikes, which is called ”carpet tack sign”. The progression of this phenomenon destroys hair follicles permanently and may result in scarring alopecia. Over time, skin lesions become atrophic with peripheral discoloration and central depigmentation and cause irreversible and severe skin defects [65].

in_text_mentions: The localized form of ACLE is commonly described as a malar or “butterfly” rash that covers the cheeks and nasal bridge (Figure 2). The forehead and anterior neck may be included, but the nasolabial folds are spared. Confluent, reddish-purple discoloration with mild edema and/or papules is common. The rash classically lasts days to weeks and can be triggered by sun exposure. It is present at diagnosis in 40-52% of SLE patients [15]. in_text_mentions: Focal hair loss is observed in telogen effluvium. Its severity is usually correlated with the activity of LE. In SLE exacerbations, excessive trichorrhexis, dryness and thinning of hair occur (Figure 10). This condition, which is dominant in the frontal hairline, is referred to as “lupus hair”. Trichoscopy may be crucial in differentiating from scarring alopecia resulting from focal lesions in the course of DLE. findings.label: Lupus nephritis class I-VI
findings.evidence: DPLN shows diffuse hypercellularity throughout the glomerulus with subendothelial immune complex deposition

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 3 panels (a, b, c). a: PAS-stained histologic section of glomerulus demonstrating diffuse proliferative lupus nephritis (DPLN) with endothelial and mesangial hypercellularity and subendothelial immune complex deposition from an SLE patient. b: PAS-stained histologic section of glomerulus demonstrating membranous lupus nephritis (MLN) with diffuse thickening of peripheral capillary walls and lack of hypercellularity from an SLE patient. c: Immunofluorescence microscopy demonstrating glomerular deposits of IgG subclasses (IgG1, IgG2, IgG3, IgG4) in a patient with membranous lupus nephritis from an SLE patient.
panels.attribution_text: Miyake et al. Th subset balance in lupus nephritis.. Journal of biomedicine & biotechnology 2011. doi:10.1155/2011/980286. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 1.
panels.figure_caption: Two polar morphologic forms are representative of histological findings in lupus nephritis. (a) DPLN shows diffuse hypercellularity of endothelial cells and mesangial cells throughout the glomerulus. Peripheral capillary are thickened by subendothelial deposition of immune complex (x400, PAS staining). (b) On the other hand MLN shows generalized diffuse thickening of the peripheral capillary walls without prominent hypercellularity in the glomerulus (x400, PAS staining). (c) Glomerular IgG subclass deposits in a patient with MLN determined by immunofluorescence microscopy (x100). IgG subclass deposition was examined using FITC-conjugated mouse antihuman IgG subclass specific mAbs.
in_text_mentions: molecules are classified into four IgG subclasses according to the immunologically distinct constant region of the heavy chain [8]. The IgG is the most important Ig isotype in immunopathogenesis for LN, and accordingly, different IgG subclasses have distinct physicochemical and biological properties. in_text_mentions: After initial diagnosis of CLE, risk of progression to SLE is between 5 and 18% within three to five years [8–10]. Approximately one-third of CLE patients have an existing diagnosis or will be diagnosed with SLE in the future [8]. Patients with ACLE, bullous lupus, and nonspecific cutaneous lesions of lupus (e.g., vasculopathic lesions, see Figure 1) all have a higher risk of developing systemic lupus when compared to individuals diagnosed with SCLE, DLE, lupus tumidus, lupus panniculitis, or chilblain lupus [1].

in_text_mentions: Cutaneous vasculitis Cutaneous vasculitis usually affects small blood vessels (leukocytoclastic vasculitis). The lesions are characterized as petechiae or palpable purpura (Figure 2A), and may occasionally blister. They are commonly found on the face, palms and soles of the feet (Figure 2B). The lesions are induced by the formation of immune complexes and neutrophilic infiltration, and the presence of vasculitic lesions strongly relates to systemic disease activity [46]. The lupus specific lesions begin with solitary erythema and hemorrhaging patches before developing into discoid ulcers with a reticulate border. Typically, the lesions are painless and located on the hard palate (Figure 2E). panels.figure_caption: Pulmonary oedema with super-added infection A 25-year-old male patient with SLE presented with complaints of fever, shortness of breath, and cough of nine-day duration. The topogram (a) revealed gross pericardial effusion and blunting of bilateral costophrenic angles (white arrows) with diffuse ground-glass haziness in bilateral lung fields. Axial (b-f) HRCT chest images in the lung window (b-d) revealed diffuse ground-glass attenuation and interlobular septal thickening in bilateral lung fields, with patchy consolidation (black arrows) in the middle lobe, right lower lobe, and left lower lobe. Topogram findings were confirmed as mild right pleural effusion (b-f, asterisk) tracking along the fissure and cardiomegaly with massive pericardial effusion (f, white arrow). Features were suggestive of pulmonary oedema with super-added infection (Pseudomonas aeruginosa). SLE: systemic lupus erythematosus; HRCT: high-resolution CT
in_text_mentions: Infection was the most common diagnosis, identified in 32 (53.3%) patients (Figures 1, 2). Among the infectious etiologies, bacterial infections were predominant, accounting for 27 (45%) cases. Other infectious causes included polymicrobial (Figure 3) and fungal infections (2 cases each, 3.3%) (Figure 4) and tubercular infection (1 case, 1.67%) (Figure 5). Pulmonary arterial hypertension was also highly prevalent, diagnosed in 30 (50%) patients. Pulmonary oedema was observed in 11 (18.3%) patients (Figures 6, 7).

panels.figure_caption: Serositis A 29-year-old female patient with SLE presented with chest pain, fever, and cough of seven-day duration. The topogram (a) revealed blunting of bilateral costophrenic angles (white arrows) with suggested loculated pleural effusion on the left side (black asterisk). Axial chest HRCT images (b-f) confirmed bilateral moderate pleural effusions (black asterisk), pericardial effusion (f, white arrows), cardiomegaly, enlarged pulmonary artery (e, white asterisk), and axillary lymphadenopathy (d, white arrow). Features were suggestive of serositis. SLE: systemic lupus erythematosus; HRCT: high-resolution CT

Less frequent diagnoses included pulmonary thromboembolism (3 cases, 5%) (Figures 12, 13), lupus pneumonitis (2 cases, 3.3%) (Figure 14), and diffuse alveolar haemorrhage (2 cases, 3.3%) (Figures 15, 16). findings.label: Malar rash (nasolabial sparing)
findings.evidence: Caption: 'Malar rash.'; in-text: erythematous rash over cheeks and nasal bridge, butterfly-shaped, sparing nasolabial folds

panels.rationale: Clinical photograph showing a classic malar (butterfly) rash, a pathognomonic cutaneous manifestation of acute cutaneous lupus erythematosus (ACLE), a subtype of systemic lupus erythematosus. The rash involves the cheeks and nasal bridge with sparing of the nasolabial folds, consistent with the described SLE-related presentation. The image is a real patient photograph with no applicable exclusions.
panels.attribution_text: Uva et al. Cutaneous manifestations of systemic lupus erythematosus.. Autoimmune diseases 2012. doi:10.1155/2012/834291. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 1.
panels.figure_caption: Malar rash.
in_text_mentions: The first criterion of the ACR is malar rash (sensitivity 57%; specificity 96%), which is characterized by an erythematous rash over the cheeks and nasal bridge (Figure 1). Malar rash is a fixed erythema that typically spares the nasolabial folds. It is a butterfly-shaped or vespertilio rash that can be flat or raised over the cheeks and bridge of the nose. It lasts from days to weeks and is occasionally painful or pruritic.

plate_findings.evidence: increased loop tortuosity

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 2 panels (a, b). a: Polarised dermoscopy (10 ×) of the proximal nailfold showing a diagnostic SLE pattern with dilated megacapillaries, increased loop tortuosity and multifocal microhaemorrhages, characteristic of systemic lupus erythematosus. b: Close-up polarised dermoscopy of the nailfold showing characteristic meandering and bushy capillary loops with associated focal microhaemorrhages (arrows), distinguishing SLE from systemic sclerosis.
panels.attribution_text: Ebaid et al. Old marker, new face: anti-RNP as a sentinel of coronary and peripheral endothelial dysfunction in systemic lupus erythematosus.. Lupus science & medicine 2026. doi:10.1136/lupus-2026-002125. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 3.
panels.figure_caption: Dermoscopic findings in SLE. (a) Polarised dermoscopy (10 ×) of the proximal nailfold showing a diagnostic ‘SLE pattern’. Key features include dilated megacapillaries, increased loop tortuosity and multifocal microhaemorrhages. These vascular distortions and areas of capillary drop-out are highly characteristic of SLE. (b) Close-up polarised dermoscopy (DermLite DL5) of the nailfold showing characteristic ‘meandering’ and ‘bushy’ capillary loops. The irregular distribution and associated focal microhaemorrhages (arrows) distinguish this pattern from the more linear, ‘comb-like’ architecture typically seen in systemic sclerosis.
in_text_mentions: Dermoscopic evaluations revealed significant associations between anti-RNP levels and peripheral microvascular changes, as shown in table 4. Higher anti-RNP levels were significantly correlated with the presence of microhaemorrhage (p=0.003), capillary dropouts (p=0.021) and mild capillary dilatation (p=0.0351) (figure 3).

findings.label: Livedo reticularis
findings.evidence: Livedo reticularis.

panels.rationale: Clinical photograph showing livedo reticularis, a recognized cutaneous manifestation of SLE, as described in an article focused on cutaneous manifestations of SLE. The image clearly displays the characteristic lace-like, mottled vascular pattern on the lower extremity.
panels.attribution_text: Uva et al. Cutaneous manifestations of systemic lupus erythematosus.. Autoimmune diseases 2012. doi:10.1155/2012/834291. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 11.
panels.figure_caption: Livedo reticularis.
in_text_mentions: Livedo reticularis is a common cutaneous reaction consisting of a mottled reticulated vascular pattern that appears like a lace-like purplish violaceous discoloration frequently on the lower extremities (Figure 11) [79]. The discoloration is caused by swelling of the medium veins in skin which makes them more visible. It can be caused by any condition that makes venules swell. The condition may be normal or may be related to severe underlying pathology. It may be aggravated by exposure to cold.

panels.rationale: Direct immunofluorescence image demonstrating lupus band test positivity with granular deposits along the dermoepidermal junction, characteristic of cutaneous lupus erythematosus in SLE patients as described in the article.

panels.figure_caption: Lupus band test.
in_text_mentions: r, when performed in the cutaneous lesions, lupus band test is positive in about 80% of patients. The fluorescent pattern of dermoepidermal skin deposits of complement or immunoglobulins are either in granules, either in thick band (Figure 12). In some SLE cases, in situ ANA deposits were observed. This pattern was first detected by Gilliam in patients with Sharp mixed connective-tissue disease but latter was shown to be not exclusive of the Sharp syndrome, but is also detected in some SLE. It corresponds to an in situ epidermis nuclear deposition of the circulating Anti-SSA of those patients.

Silver: Silver stain of glomeruli showing characteristic double contour (tram track)...
panels.attribution_text: Sterner et al. The Pathogenesis of Lupus Nephritis.. Journal of clinical & cellular immunology 2014. doi:10.4172/2155-9899.1000205. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 2.
panels.figure_caption: Characteristic histopathologic manifestations of diffuse proliferative lupus nephritis (Class IV-G/A by the International Society of Nephrology/Renal Pathology Society Classification). Glomeruli (left column) are diffusely hyper-cellular. Peripheral capillary loop lumens are compromised due to endocapillary proliferation (arrow). Large immune complex deposits are observed between layers of basement membrane material (silver stain, middle, arrow) giving rise to the characteristic “tram track” or double contour appearance of the capillary loops. Immunofluorescence studies demonstrate the characteristic “full house” pattern of positive staining for all immune reactants (IgG, IgA, IgM, C1q, C3, kappa and lambda light chain) in glomeruli.
in_text_mentions: sinuating that Ccr1 is important for the recruitment of T cells and mononuclear phagocyte cells [70]. CD147 is a glycosylated transmembrane protein that plays a role in regulating lymphocyte response and leukocyte influx, it is induced in injured glomeruli and incoming inflammatory cells, and plasma levels reflect histological disease activity, making it a good potential biomarker in lupus nephritis patients [71] (Figure 2). The presence of greater than or equal to 800/100 mL of CD4+ T cells in urine is a sensitive and specific biomarker for active proliferative nephritis in SLE patients [72].

Within the ILD subset, nonspecific interstitial pneumonia (NSIP) was the most common pattern (4 cases, 6.6%) (Figure 9), followed by organising pneumonia (2 cases, 3.3%) (Figures 10, 11). Sequelae of old infection were identified in 5 (8.3%) cases. in_text_mentions: Infection was the most common diagnosis, identified in 32 (53.3%) patients (Figures 1, 2). Among the infectious etiologies, bacterial infections were predominant, accounting for 27 (45%) cases. Other infectious causes included polymicrobial (Figure 3) and fungal infections (2 cases each, 3.3%) (Figure 4) and tubercular infection (1 case, 1.67%) (Figure 5). Pulmonary arterial hypertension was also highly prevalent, diagnosed in 30 (50%) patients. Pulmonary oedema was observed in 11 (18.3%) patients (Figures 6, 7).

plate_findings.evidence: PAS-stained glomeruli from lupus nephritis patient biopsy or autopsy specimens

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 3 panels (A, B, C). A: Real patient renal histology (PAS stain) from lupus nephritis patients showing glomerular morphology consistent with lupus nephritis, a subtype of systemic lupus erythematosus. B: Real patient renal immunofluorescence images from lupus nephritis patients demonstrating co-localization of autoantigen RRP8 with IgG/C3 in glomerular regions, consistent with lupus nephritis. C: Real patient renal immunofluorescence images from lupus nephritis patients demonstrating co-localization of autoantigen TNP1 with IgG/C3 along the glomerular basement membrane, consistent with lupus nephritis.
panels.attribution_text: Onishi et al. Novel Autoantigens Associated with Lupus Nephritis.. PloS one 2015. doi:10.1371/journal.pone.0126564. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 2.
panels.figure_caption: Double immunofluorescence of RRP8 or TNP1 and IgG or C3 in renal sections from patients with LN. Formalin-fixed, paraffin-embedded sections of biopsy or autopsy specimens from LN patients were processed for double immunofluorescence staining. Representative photographs are shown. The specimens were stained with Alexa 546-conjugated anti-RRP8 or anti-TNP1 antibodies (red) and with FITC-conjugated anti-IgG or anti-C3 antibodies (green). (A) The same glomeruli were stained with periodic acid-Schiff. (B) Co-presence of RRP8 and C3 was detected along the sub-epithelial area of the glomeruli showing a dotted pattern (arrowhead) in LN1. Also in Autopsy1, both RRP8 and IgG signals were detected in the mesangial area as well as in the sub-epithelial area (arrowhead). (C) Co-presence of TNP1 and IgG was revealed along the basement membrane showing a linear pattern in LN2, as was the case for TNP1 and C3 in Autopsy2. The bold and strong autofluorescence in each of the panels is mainly due to red blood cells.
in_text_mentions: this study. Paraffin sections, and not frozen sections, were used as no frozen sections had been stocked. plate_findings.evidence: H&E ×200 showing diffuse thickening of glomerular basement membranes in lupus-like membranous glomerulopathy
IgG ×400 granular deposits along glomerular capillary basement membranes

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 10 panels ((a) A, (a) B, (a) C, (a) D, (a) E, (b) A, (b) B, (b) C, (b) D, (b) E). (a) A: Histologic image showing lupus-like membranous glomerulopathy with thickened glomerular basement membranes, characteristic of lupus nephritis (Class V) pathology. (a) B: Histologic image confirming lupus-like membranous glomerulopathy with PAS staining highlighting basement membrane thickening. (a) C: Immunohistochemistry showing C4d deposition along GBM, supporting lupus-like pathology. (a) D: Negative IgG4 staining helps distinguish lupus-like membranous glomerulopathy from primary membranous nephropathy. panels.figure_caption: Diffuse alveolar haemorrhage A 27-year-old female patient with SLE presented with complaints of shortness of breath, fever, chest pain, and cough of four-day duration. Axial (a-c) and coronal (d) HRCT chest images in the lung window revealed symmetrical ground-glass opacities in both central and peripheral lung fields. Additionally, in the mediastinal window (e, f), an enlarged pulmonary artery (asterisk), mild pericardial (f, arrowhead) and bilateral pleural effusions (f, arrows), and cardiomegaly were also noted. Incidentally, vascular calcifications were observed in both breasts (e, arrows). Findings were consistent with diffuse alveolar haemorrhage. SLE: systemic lupus erythematosus; HRCT: high-resolution CT
in_text_mentions: were each noted in 6 (10%) patients. Within the ILD subset, nonspecific interstitial pneumonia (NSIP) was the most common pattern (4 cases, 6.6%) (Figure 9), followed by organising pneumonia (2 cases, 3.3%) (Figures 10, 11). Sequelae of old infection were identified in 5 (8.3%) cases. Less frequent diagnoses included pulmonary thromboembolism (3 cases, 5%) (Figures 12, 13), lupus pneumonitis (2 cases, 3.3%) (Figure 14), and diffuse alveolar haemorrhage (2 cases, 3.3%) (Figures 15, 16). No cases of shrinking lung syndrome or neoplastic conditions were observed in the study population (Table 3).

Cardiac involvement is a less common systemic manifestation of SLE, so the presentation is classified as variant.

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 6 panels (a, b, c, d, e, f). a: Caption explicitly identifies this T2-weighted MRI panel as cerebellar infarction in a 14-year-old with NPSLE, with swelling causing fourth-ventricle compression and mild hydrocephalus. b: The caption explicitly attributes the brainstem lesion to infarction in a patient with NPSLE. c: Caption and arrow identify infarction in the right posterior thalamus in a 14-year-old with NPSLE. d: Caption identifies diffusion-weighted hyperintensity as an acute infarct associated with the documented NPSLE cerebral infarction. e: MRA signal void at the distal basilar artery is explicitly captioned as a large-vessel occlusion in the NPSLE case. f: The panel directly demonstrates multiple deep frontal white-matter lesions, and the article and caption identify them as borderzone infarcts in juvenile-onset NPSLE.
panels.attribution_text: Al-Obaidi et al. Evaluation of magnetic resonance imaging abnormalities in juvenile onset neuropsychiatric systemic lupus erythematosus.. Clinical rheumatology 2016. doi:10.1007/s10067-016-3376-9. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 2.
panels.figure_caption: Infarction in a 14 year old with NPSLE of the a cerebellum, b brainstem, and c right posterior thalamus (arrow) diagnosed on the T2-weighted MR images. Cerebellar swelling compressing the fourth ventricle resulted in mild hydrocephalus. d The diffusion-weighted imaging revealed a high signal lesion in keeping with an acute infarct. e A signal void of the distal basilar artery (white arrow) on the MRA of the posterior circulation revealed a large vessel occlusion. f Multiple borderzone infarcts are seen within the deep white matter of the frontal lobes, some of which were acute. The anterior circulation was normal (not shown)
in_text_mentions: and sizes. One child had an acute basilar artery occlusion resulting in infarction of the cerebellum, brainstem, posterior thalamus on the right and mild hydrocephalus with restricted diffusion (Fig. 2). Of the remaining, white matter hyperintensity lesions occurred in the supratentorial white matter in 7/8 patients (88.9 %), in the brainstem in one patient (11.1 %). Multiple white matter lesions these were distributed asymmetrically. White matter lesions were present in patients with all types of ACR-defined NPSLE syndromes in this study (Table 2).Fig. 2Infarction in a 14 year old with NPSLE

Another child had an extensive acute infarction of the midbrain and both cerebellar hemispheres with ischaemic change in the deep white matter watershed regions of both cerebral hemispheres, body of the corpus callosum and left parietal cortex (Fig. 2). MRA revealed occlusion of the distal basilar artery.

in_text_mentions: SCLE was predominantly characterized by a polymorphous vascular pattern (92.6%) of unspecific distribution (92.6%) over a pink-red background (74.1%). Of note, gray-brown dots were present in 10 (37.0%) cases, and pigmentation in 15 (55.6%) patients. Peripheral pigmentation was observed in seven (25.9%) patients (Table 2). Sample dermoscopic images are provided in Figure 1.

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 4 panels (A, B, C, D). A: Clinical photograph of a 23-year-old SLE patient showing malar erythema involving the cheeks and nose, a classic acute cutaneous lupus erythematosus (ACLE) manifestation, with annotation overlays marking erythema severity scores. B: Clinical photograph of a 23-year-old SLE patient showing erythema on the fingertips, a non-specific cutaneous SLE manifestation, with annotation overlays marking erythema. C: Clinical photograph of a 23-year-old SLE patient showing non-scarring alopecia of the scalp, a classic SLE cutaneous manifestation, with annotation overlay marking the alopecic area. D: Clinical photograph of a 23-year-old SLE patient showing bilateral arm lesions with erythema, scale, scarring, and dyspigmentation, classic features of discoid lupus erythematosus (DLE) plaques, with annotation overlays marking each feature's severity score.

panels.figure_caption: Representative images of cutaneous lesions with various severity of SLE and scoring criteria. A–D An example of the cutaneous lesions in the study represented images of a 23-year-old female. A Erythema was graded as score 3 on the both cheeks and score 1 on the nose, thus giving a total score of 4 for erythema in the face. B Erythema was graded as score 1 on the four fingertips of the both hands. C Alopecia was graded as score 1 in hairy areas of the scalp. D Erythema, scale, scarring, and dyspigmentation were graded as respective scores of 3, 1, 1, and 1 on both arms, thus giving a total score of 6 in arms. In total, CLASI activity score of 10 and CLASI damage score of 2 reflect the extent of cutaneous lesions. Red: erythema; green: scale; blue: alopecia; yellow: scarring; black: dyspigmentation

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 5 panels (A, B, C, D, E). A: Clinical photo of patient with monogenic SLE showing classic discoid lupus erythematosus manifestations including occipital scarring alopecia and palmoplantar erosive plaques. B: Brain MRI of patient with monogenic SLE showing neuropsychiatric SLE white-matter lesions as described in the caption. C: Clinical photos of patient with monogenic SLE showing subacute cutaneous lupus erythematosus papulosquamous abdominal rash and palmar erythema. D: Lung wedge biopsy histology shows SLE-related pneumonitis findings, but none match the required allowed findings vocabulary, so the panel is excluded per rule 6. E: Chest CT shows aortic dilation and calcifications related to SLE, but these findings are not present in the required allowed findings vocabulary, so the panel is excluded per rule 6.
panels.attribution_text: Tirosh et al. Whole exome sequencing in childhood-onset lupus frequently detects single gene etiologies.. Pediatric rheumatology online journal 2019. doi:10.1186/s12969-019-0349-y. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 1.
panels.figure_caption: Representative clinical findings in patients with monogenic SLE. Panel A – Occipital and lower extremities lesions noted in patients 1A with C1QC mutation, reveals palmoplantar erosive erythemic plaques and scarring alopecia. Panel B – Abnormal brain MRI scan of patient 2B with PTEN mutation shows non-specific parieto-occipital lesions affecting the white matter and cortical dysplasia. Panel C – Patient 3C with SLC7A7 and MAN2B1 mutations, exhibits a palmar erythema and diffuse abdominal papulosquamous rash. Panel D – Lung wedge biopsy of patient 3C shows: (a) sheets of large vacuolated macrophages in the interstitium (asterisks) and eosinophilic intra-alveolar exudate (arrow) H&E X 100. (b) The intra-alveolar exudate contains cholesterol clefts and it is PAS-positive and diastase resistant (PAS-diastase stain X 200). (c) Mild- to moderate alveolar wall thickening (H&E × 100). (d) Mild fibrosis (Masson trichrome stain × 100). (e) Diffuse inflammatory T-cell infiltration (CD3 immunostain × 200). (f) B- cell aggregates (CD20 immunostain × 200). (g) Part of alveolar spaces contain hemosiderin laden macrophages (Prussian blue stain × 200). Panel E – Chest CT angiography in patient 4D with STAT1 gain of function mutation, shows dilated ascending aorta with severe calcifications

At the age of 2 years, during tapering of steroid therapy, she developed daily fever, malar rash, severe digital and oral ulcers, arthritis and gastrointestinal bleeding. Lumbar puncture demonstrated pleocytosis, high protein level and low glucose levels. Cerebrospinal fluid studies were negative for viral, bacterial, or fungal infections. He was treated with pulse doses of methylprednisolone, intravenous cyclophosphamide and Rituximab, but had a poor response. in_text_mentions: Histopathological examination revealed a dense lymphocytic inflammatory infiltrate distributed in a perivascular and periadnexal pattern involving both the superficial and deep dermis (Figure 3). These findings were consistent with a diagnosis of LET.

findings.label: Wire-loop lesion
findings.evidence: subendothelial deposits ('wire loops')

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 3 panels (a, b, c). a: Panel a shows a trichrome-stained renal biopsy with wire-loop lesions and endocapillary hypercellularity characteristic of lupus nephritis. b: Panel b shows a silver methenamine-stained renal biopsy with spikes corresponding to subepithelial deposits, consistent with lupus nephritis. c: Panel c shows immunofluorescence of a renal biopsy demonstrating the full-house pattern pathognomonic for lupus nephritis.
panels.attribution_text: Santos et al. Lupus-like nephritis with positive anti-neutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies and negative antinuclear antibodies.. Jornal brasileiro de nefrologia 2022. doi:10.1590/2175-8239-jbn-2020-0114. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 1.
panels.figure_caption: Image a (trichrome stain, x400) and b (silver methenamine stain, x400) shows endocapillary hypercellularity and prominent subendothelial deposits ("wire loops"). It shows a lobular expansion and increases of mesangial matrix, imparting a membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis-like appearance. We can see also global and diffuse thickening of the glomerular basal membrane with granular subepithelial deposits (mainly in trichrome) with silver-positive spikes. Tubules and interstitium present with extended mononuclear infiltrate and 60% of tubulointerstitial fibrosis. Image c (immunofluorescence, x400) shows IgG parietal granular deposits in glomeruli accompanied by IgA, IgM, C3, C1q, kappa, and lambda deposits in a full-house pattern.
in_text_mentions: Kidney biopsy (Figure 1) was performed, revealing active global endocapillary and mesangial hypercellularity, and a diffuse thickening of the glomerular wall with "spikes" on light microscopy. On immunofluorescence there were diffuse mesangial, subendothelial, and subepithelial immune deposits, in "full-house nephropathy" pattern. The pathological diagnosis was consistent with class IVa and V LN.

panels.stage: class IV and class V lupus nephritis
panels.rationale: This is a renal-biopsy immunofluorescence image from a human patient with lupus nephritis. The caption directly documents granular glomerular IgG deposition in subepithelial, focal subendothelial, and mesangial locations, while the article explicitly attributes the biopsy findings to lupus nephritis.
panels.attribution_text: Sawant et al. Silent Storm Unveiled: Lupus Nephritis and Cerebral Vasculitis in Systemic Lupus Erythematosus.. Cureus 2024. doi:10.7759/cureus.57751. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 5.
panels.figure_caption: Immunofluorescence microscopy (IgG, 40X). The IF image is showing a glomerulus with diffuse fine granular deposits of 2+ to 3+ intensity along the GBM, indicative of subepithelial immune deposits. These deposits were seen over >50% of the total GBM area. Few segments show linear interrupted/semi-linear deposits along the GBM indicative of subendothelial immune deposits. Segmental mesangial deposits were also present. IgG: immunoglobulin G, GBM: glomerular basement membrane
in_text_mentions: With the 24-hour urinary protein level elevated at 650 mg/day, suspicion of LN arose, prompting a renal biopsy for further evaluation. The biopsy results revealed a combination of class IV diffuse proliferative glomerulonephritis and class V membranous nephropathy, thereby confirming the diagnosis of LN (Figures 4, 5). A chest X-ray was done, which suggested bilateral pleural effusion (Figure 6). Her sputum examination was done, cultures showed no growth or organism, and her GeneXpert did not detect mycobacterium tuberculosis.

in_text_mentions: With the 24-hour urinary protein level elevated at 650 mg/day, suspicion of LN arose, prompting a renal biopsy for further evaluation. The biopsy results revealed a combination of class IV diffuse proliferative glomerulonephritis and class V membranous nephropathy, thereby confirming the diagnosis of LN (Figures 4, 5). A chest X-ray was done, which suggested bilateral pleural effusion (Figure 6). Her sputum examination was done, cultures showed no growth or organism, and her GeneXpert did not detect mycobacterium tuberculosis.

in_text_mentions: E) was done, which showed a left ventricular ejection fraction of 65%, severe left ventricular hypertrophy, moderate pericardial effusion, and moderately thickened mitral valve (MV) leaflets (Figures 2, 3). She was admitted to the Neurology intensive care unit for stroke management and was started on aspirin, atorvastatin, and a heparin drip. The patient did not receive alteplase for being out of the time window and having an ASPECTS (Alberta stroke program early CT score) of 6 was unfavorable for thrombectomy. The rheumatology service was consulted for the medical management of lupus in the s

e, with a history of SLE on HCQ, experienced a stroke with M1 middle cerebral artery occlusion (Figure 1), indicating a likely embolic arterial source. To find the source of the embolus, a transthoracic echocardiogram (TTE) was conducted and revealed severe left ventricular hypertrophy (LVH) with preserved left ventricular ejection fraction (65%) (Figures 2, 3). Considering this finding and knowledge of several case reports noting the rare risk of HCQ-induced hypertrophic cardiomyopathy and its complications, we believe that the medication is the cause of the hypertrophy in this young patient.

The captioned lichenoid infiltrate at the dermal-epidermal junction and interstitial mucin are characteristic histologic manifestations supporting cutaneous lupus.

panels.figure_caption: A punch biopsy at 40x magnification showing dense lichenoid infiltrate along the dermal-epidermal junction with perivascular and periadnexal accentuation and interstitial mucin deposition.
in_text_mentions: Physical exam revealed erythematous, ovoid plaques on the shoulders, and an erythematous papulosquamous eruption which coalesced to form large patches on the chest, shoulders, and upper back (Figure 1). Scattered erythematous macules with fine scales were present on the scalp. A punch biopsy of the left trapezius revealed colloid bodies, a lichenified lymphocytic infiltrate along the dermal-epidermal junction, and interstitial deposits of mucin (Figures 2, 3).

She was commenced on oral prednisolone 50 mg daily, oral rabeprazole 20 mg daily, oral hydroxychloroquine 200 mg twice daily, oral calcium/vitamin D supplementation, haematinics, oral atorvastatin 10 mg daily, and oral lisinopril 5 mg daily. in_text_mentions: ined in electron microscopy, one of which was globally sclerotic. The others showed the presence of massive para-mesangial and subendothelial deposits with a moderate fusion of pedicels of podocytes [Figure 3]. Given the findings of mesangial deposits with increased mesangial cellularity and a predominance of IgA and C3 deposits in immunofluorescence microscopy, this was classified as IgA nephropathy, based on the Oxford classification, with a score of M0 E1 S1 T1 C2. findings.evidence: Caption describes a classic confluent, erythematous malar rash over the malar eminences and nasal bridge with nasolabial fold sparing, a hallmark of SLE.

panels.rationale: Single clinical photograph of a patient with active SLE showing a classic malar (butterfly) rash, the defining cutaneous manifestation of acute cutaneous lupus erythematosus (ACLE), with no exclusions applicable.

panels.figure_caption: Malar (“Butterfly”) rash characteristic of systemic lupus erythematosus. A clinical photograph of the patient's face upon admission, showing a classic confluent, erythematous rash over the malar eminences and the bridge of the nose, with notable sparing of the nasolabial folds. This is a hallmark cutaneous manifestation of active jSLE.
in_text_mentions: Her neurological status was intact with a Glasgow Coma Score (GCS) of 15. Dermatological examination revealed a confluent erythematous rash over the nasal bridge and malar eminences, consistent with a “butterfly rash” (Figure 1), along with discoid lesions on the pinnae. Her palms and soles showed erythematous macules (Figures 2, 3, 4). Abdominal examination was notable for marked tenderness to deep palpation in the epigastrium, without guarding or rebound tenderness.

plate_findings.evidence: full-house pattern

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 5 panels (A, B, C, D, E). A: Light microscopy image showing a fibrocellular crescent, a characteristic feature of proliferative (class IV) lupus nephritis, from a renal biopsy of a patient with mixed class IV+V lupus nephritis. B: Light microscopy image demonstrating endocapillary hypercellularity with active proliferative lesions, consistent with class IV lupus nephritis activity. C: Light microscopy image showing segmental glomerulosclerosis, a chronicity feature seen in lupus nephritis. D: Silver stain demonstrating glomerular basement membrane spikes and holes, consistent with membranous (class V) features in mixed lupus nephritis. E: Immunofluorescence image demonstrating C3-dominant immune complex deposition with a full-house pattern, characteristic of lupus nephritis.

findings.evidence: Caption states 'suggestive of early scarring alopecia'; in-text mentions 'early scarring alopecia'

panels.rationale: Clinical photograph of a pediatric patient's scalp showing a localized alopecic patch with reduced follicular openings and smooth surface, consistent with early scarring alopecia in lupus erythematosus profundus, a recognized cutaneous manifestation of systemic lupus erythematosus.
panels.attribution_text: Almoosawi et al. A Unique Case of Lupus Erythematosus Profundus Presenting With Localized Scarring Alopecia and Perioral Swelling in a Pediatric Patient.. Cureus 2026. doi:10.7759/cureus.105300. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 1.
panels.figure_caption: Localized alopecic patch over the left parietal scalp measuring approximately 4 × 2 cm, with reduced follicular openings suggestive of early scarring alopecia
in_text_mentions: able, and had age-appropriate growth parameters. Cutaneous examination demonstrated a localized alopecic patch over the left parietal scalp measuring approximately 4 × 2 cm. The surface was smooth with reduced follicular openings and without appreciable scale, crust, pustulation, ulceration, or discharge. The lesion appeared clinically indurated rather than fluctuant and was most consistent with an early inflammatory cicatricial process. Figure 1 shows the scalp lesion. Trichoscopy demonstrated decreased follicular density and areas of absent follicles, in keeping with early scarring alopecia.

findings.label: Oral/palatal ulcer
findings.evidence: Oral ulcer on the left posterior palate at the time of presentation

panels.rationale: Clinical photograph of a discrete oral ulcer on the posterior palate in a patient with juvenile systemic lupus erythematosus, a classic recognized mucocutaneous manifestation of SLE. The image is a real patient clinical photo with clear, supported disease attribution and specific finding.
panels.attribution_text: Schildt et al. Juvenile Systemic Lupus Erythematosus Presenting with Esophagitis and Severe Oral Mucositis.. Case reports in rheumatology 2021. doi:10.1155/2021/5868655. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 2.
panels.figure_caption: Oral ulcer on the left posterior palate at the time of presentation.
in_text_mentions: Her exam was significant for diffusely edematous and erythematous upper and lower lips with cracking, blistering, and evidence of prior bleeding (Figure 1). She had erythema and dried blood visible on her upper and lower gingivae without discrete lesions. She additionally had a 5 mm dark red ulceration on her posterior palate (Figure 2). No aphthous ulcerations or vesicular lesions were present on her oral mucosa. She had no nasal, labial, or perianal mucosal changes and no skin rashes. Her joints were unremarkable without swelling, pain, or stiffness.
panels.copyright: Schildt et al. Juvenile Systemic Lupus Erythematosus Presenting with Esophagitis and Severe Oral Mucositis.. Case reports in rheumatology 2021. doi:10.1155/2021/5868655. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 2.

in_text_mentions: Her neurological status was intact with a Glasgow Coma Score (GCS) of 15. Dermatological examination revealed a confluent erythematous rash over the nasal bridge and malar eminences, consistent with a “butterfly rash” (Figure 1), along with discoid lesions on the pinnae. Her palms and soles showed erythematous macules (Figures 2, 3, 4). Abdominal examination was notable for marked tenderness to deep palpation in the epigastrium, without guarding or rebound tenderness.

findings.evidence: bilateral pleural effusions

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 2 panels (A, B). A: Chest X-ray from a septuagenarian SLE patient demonstrating bilateral pleural and pericardial effusions and pulmonary infiltrates (cotton-wool), consistent with systemic lupus erythematosus with cardiopulmonary involvement. B: Lung ultrasound from the same SLE patient showing a large left pleural effusion, consistent with lupus pleuritis.
panels.attribution_text: Angulo et al. Massive Pericardial Effusion and Type 3 Cardiorenal Syndrome as the Inaugural Presentation of Late-Onset Systemic Lupus Erythematosus in a Septuagenarian.. Cureus 2026. doi:10.7759/cureus.102066. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 1.
panels.figure_caption: (A) Anteroposterior chest X-ray demonstrating cotton-wool infiltrates (arrows), cardiomegaly, and bilateral pericardial and pleural effusions. (B) Lung ultrasound image showing a large, 1000 mL left pleural effusion (arrow)
in_text_mentions: (28 mm) was noted, exhibiting the "swinging heart" phenomenon. Significant signs of cardiac pre-tamponade were present, including diastolic collapse of the right atrium, dilated inferior vena cava without inspiratory collapse, and marked respiratory variation in transmitral (>30%) and transtricuspid (>25%) flows. Chest radiography demonstrated cardiomegaly, bilateral cotton-wool infiltrates, and bilateral pleural effusions. She was transferred to the intensive care unit for vasoactive support and underwent ultrasound-guided pericardiocentesis, draining 800 mL of transudative fluid (Figure 1).

in_text_mentions: At the age of two, a purple rash appeared on the back of his hands, on the tip of all his fingers and his ear lobes. There was no history of fever, arthritis, alopecia, oral lesions, or respiratory or gastrointestinal symptoms. On admission, he appeared well. He had dysmorphic facial features. Vasculitic lesions were observed on the back of his hands, ear lobes, feet and fingertips (Figure 1a - 1b). The rest of the physical examination was normal.

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 2 panels (a, b). a: Apical four-chamber echocardiogram view showing pericardial effusion in a patient with systemic lupus erythematosus presenting with myopericarditis. b: Subcostal four-chamber echocardiogram view showing pericardial effusion in a patient with systemic lupus erythematosus presenting with myopericarditis.
panels.attribution_text: Durrance et al. Systemic Lupus Erythematosus Presenting as Myopericarditis with Acute Heart Failure: A Case Report and Literature Review.. Case reports in rheumatology 2019. doi:10.1155/2019/6173276. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 3.
panels.figure_caption: Transthoracic ultrasound on admission: (a) apical four-chamber view and (b) subcostal four-chamber view showing a large pericardial effusion and dilated cavities. On Doppler and dynamic views, global hypokinesis and severe mitral regurgitation were appreciated (RA = right atrium; RV = right ventricle; LA = left atrium; LV = left ventricle).
in_text_mentions: diogram was done on hospital day 1, and confirmed the presence of a significantly dilated right ventricle, severe tricuspid, and moderate mitral regurgitation with no valvular structural abnormalities described. In addition, a moderately compromised left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) (30–40%) and a large pericardial effusion (Figure 3) were shown. CT of the chest with pulmonary artery protocol was not supportive of pulmonary embolism as the underlying etiology. While the syndromic diagnosis of dilated cardiomyopathy with right sided heart failure was made, the etiology remained unknown.

panels.rationale: The echocardiogram is a real patient image showing pericardial and left pleural effusions with mobile intrapericardial fibrinous strands, attributed in the caption and article to systemic lupus erythematosus presenting with cardiac tamponade.

in_text_mentions: chocardiography confirmed features of cardiac tamponade from a large circumferential pericardial effusion, along with mobile intrapericardial fibrinous strands and the pleural effusion [Figures 3 and 4].Figure 1 Electrical alternans was clearly evidenced by the alternating amplitude of the QRS complexes (arrows). Figure 2 Posteroanterior chest radiograph at presentation revealed a markedly enlarged cardiac silhouette and a left-sided pulmonary infiltrate. Figure 3 Two-dimensional transthoracic echocardiography visualized a large circumferential pericardial effusion (PE). Figure 4 Two-dimension

as it can also grade and localize the pericardial effusion, detect pericardial thickening and visualize intrapericardial adhesions. In our patient echocardiography clearly visualized a large circumferential pericardial effusion with characteristic signs of tamponade and also confirmed a left-sided pleural effusion. Within the pericardial effusion, there were partially attached mobile fibrinous strands traversing the visceral and parietal pericardium (Figure 4). This visually dramatic feature has been reported in similar aSLE cases and may be a harbinger of difficult pericardiocentesis [15-17].

Deposits are demonstrable, although their precise lupus nephritis class is not stated in the caption.

in_text_mentions: ermittent hemodialysis was initiated on day 6, and a kidney biopsy was performed. It showed 11 glomeruli, all of them with degenerated and hypertrophic podocytes. One glomerulus presented with a segmental collapse of capillary walls. Renal interstitium showed dilated tubules filled with hyaline casts, mild fibrosis, and tubular atrophy (Figure 1). Immunofluorescence microscopy showed segmental and irregular IgM (++/4+) and C3 (traces) deposits. By electron microscopy, mild mesangial and sparse subepithelial deposits were seen associated with capillary wall retraction and tortuosity (Figure 2).

The image shows multiple discoid annular skin lesions on the head, and the article identifies these as neonatal lupus lesions.

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 2 panels (a, b). a: Real neonatal clinical photographs in a case report of siblings with neonatal lupus erythematosus. Panel a specifically shows inflammatory annular plaques with atrophic centers and hyperkeratotic borders, supporting cutaneous lupus involvement. b: Real neonatal clinical photograph showing multiple plantar discoid lesions, explicitly attributed in the caption to neonatal lupus erythematosus. Plantar involvement is rare but is specifically captioned as an indicator of potential systemic involvement.
panels.attribution_text: Tang et al. Case Report: Siblings with neonatal lupus erythematosus.. Frontiers in pediatrics 2025. doi:10.3389/fped.2025.1518881. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 1.
panels.figure_caption: (a) Case 1: clinical appearances of head lesions: inflammatory annular plaques, with hyperkeratotic borders and atrophic centers. The alopecia spot on the right side of the head was due to shave by healthcare workers, which could expose the superficial vein of the scalp (yellow arrow), for the purpose of taking blood tests. (b) Case 1: multiple discoid skin lesions on the left plantar. Despite their rarity in NLE, plantar lesions are significant indicators of potential systemic involvement, requiring comprehensive evaluations and appropriate management for a favorable prognosis (21).
in_text_mentions: ) presented with erythema on her body. Born via vaginal delivery at 40 weeks to a 29-year-old mother, she exhibited targetoid erythematous plaques with central atrophy and raised margins on her face (Figure 1a), trunk, extremities, palms, and soles (Figure 1b). Laboratory tests indicated that the liver and kidney functions and the complete blood count were normal. Serologic tests revealed strongly positive SSA (Ro) and SSB (La) antibodies, a reactive ANA titer of 1:1000 with a speckled nuclear pattern by indirect immunofluorescence (IIF), and a negative syphilis test. findings.label: Interface dermatitis
findings.evidence: Caption: "A 2x low-power hematoxylin & eosin staining - interface dermatitis"

panels.rationale: Low-power H&E biopsy from a representative lesion described in the article as supporting tumid lupus. The directly depicted finding is interface dermatitis, with deep perivascular and periadnexal lymphoplasmacytic inflammation indicated by arrows. Tumid lupus is not a separately configured subtype, so it is assigned to other_systemic.
panels.attribution_text: Aung and Celestin. Chilblains With Tumid Lupus Features in a Patient With Sjögren's Syndrome: A Case Report.. Cureus 2025. doi:10.7759/cureus.82439. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 4.
panels.figure_caption: A 2x low-power hematoxylin & eosin staining - interface dermatitis, with arrows showing deep perivascular and periadnexal lymphoplasmacytic inflammation
in_text_mentions: A punch biopsy from a representative lesion on the right paraspinal back demonstrated interface dermatitis with superficial and deep dermal perivascular and perifollicular lymphoplasmacytic inflammation (Figures 4-5). Special stains (alcian blue and colloidal iron) revealed increased dermal mucin deposition (Figure 6). No evidence of malignancy was identified. The pathologist commented that the findings supported a diagnosis of connective tissue disease, most consistent with tumid lupus.

findings.label: Livedo reticularis
findings.evidence: Caption: 'non-scaly pink thin plaques in a livedo reticularis-like pattern'

panels.rationale: This is a clinical photograph of a real human patient showing a skin eruption consistent with lupus erythematosus tumidus, a subtype of systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) present in the patient described in the article. The caption and in-text describe the lesion as non-scaly pink plaques with a livedo reticularis-like pattern on the left lower back, which matches the visible content of the image. No exclusion criteria apply, and the disease attribution and visible findings are well-supported by the provided context.
panels.attribution_text: Logothetis et al. Development of Lupus Erythematosus Tumidus During the Course of Systemic Sclerosis.. Cureus 2021. doi:10.7759/cureus.18064. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 2.
panels.figure_caption: Left lower back eruption consisting of non-scaly pink thin plaques in a livedo reticularis-like pattern.
in_text_mentions: His SS and pulmonary fibrosis had been stable without the use of immune modulators until 2014 when he developed pulmonary hypertension and was placed on hydroxychloroquine. In 2015, he developed photosensitive erythematous lesions located on the upper part of his trunk and neck. The eruption consisted of succulent, non-scaly pink elevated plaques on the trunk, which seemed to resemble a livedo reticularis-like pattern (Figure 2).

ash (petechiae) in the legs. The left lower leg circumference (mid-thigh) was +1.5 cm than the right one, painful on palpation. This is a cardiac manifestation of SLE, classified under the other-systemic subtype.

in_text_mentions: was done, which showed a left ventricular ejection fraction of 65%, severe left ventricular hypertrophy, moderate pericardial effusion, and moderately thickened mitral valve (MV) leaflets (Figures 2, 3). She was admitted to the Neurology intensive care unit for stroke management and was started on aspirin, atorvastatin, and a heparin drip. The patient did not receive alteplase for being out of the time window and having an ASPECTS (Alberta stroke program early CT score) of 6 was unfavorable for thrombectomy. The rheumatology service was consulted for the medical management of lupus in the sett

e, with a history of SLE on HCQ, experienced a stroke with M1 middle cerebral artery occlusion (Figure 1), indicating a likely embolic arterial source. To find the source of the embolus, a transthoracic echocardiogram (TTE) was conducted and revealed severe left ventricular hypertrophy (LVH) with preserved left ventricular ejection fraction (65%) (Figures 2, 3). Considering this finding and knowledge of several case reports noting the rare risk of HCQ-induced hypertrophic cardiomyopathy and its complications, we believe that the medication is the cause of the hypertrophy in this young patient.

in_text_mentions: h luminal occlusion, fibrin deposition, and fragmented RBCs. Immunofluorescence showed granular immunostain deposits of IgA, IgG, IgM, C3, C1q kappa, and lambda. Fibrinogen immunostaining showed 3+ positivity in the glomerular thrombi, confirming the presence of fibrin deposits. However, the vessels did not show any immune deposits. Correlating the histomorphology and immunofluorescence findings, a diagnosis of class IV LN with thrombotic microangiopathy was favored following the ISN/RPS classification. The activity and chronicity indices scores were 14/24 and 5/12, respectively (Figures 2-3).

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 3 panels (A, B, C). A: Renal H&E micrograph from a pediatric patient with class IV lupus nephritis showing captioned glomerular capillary and microangiopathic changes. B: Renal H&E micrograph showing the captioned thrombotic microangiopathy attributed to class IV lupus nephritis in a pediatric patient. C: Renal H&E micrograph explicitly captioned as a diffuse lupus nephritis lesion in a pediatric patient with systemic lupus erythematosus.

panels.figure_caption: Light microscopy evaluation A: Glomerular capillary congestion, endothelial swelling and necrosis and glomerular capillary thrombosis with entrapment of fragmented erythrocytes (H&E, 200x); B: Vessel wall with luminal occlusion, fibrin deposition and fragmented RBCs (H&E, 200x); C: Diffuse LN lesion in glomerulus (H&E, 200x) H&E: Hematoxylin and eosin, LN: Lupus nephritis
in_text_mentions: h luminal occlusion, fibrin deposition, and fragmented RBCs. Immunofluorescence showed granular immunostain deposits of IgA, IgG, IgM, C3, C1q kappa, and lambda. Fibrinogen immunostaining showed 3+ positivity in the glomerular thrombi, confirming the presence of fibrin deposits. However, the vessels did not show any immune deposits. Correlating the histomorphology and immunofluorescence findings, a diagnosis of class IV LN with thrombotic microangiopathy was favored following the ISN/RPS classification. The activity and chronicity indices scores were 14/24 and 5/12, respectively (Figures 2-3).

in_text_mentions: A 27-year-old primgravida in her Second trimester, sought care at the internal medicine outpatient clinic with a history of persistent non itchy maculopapular rash on her lower limbs and back, oral aphthous ulcer, arthritis and malar rash (Fig. 1) exacerbated by sunlight exposure and hot weather. Concurrently, she reported symmetrical and bilateral arthritis mainly affecting the knee and elbow joints and morning stiffness. Her symptoms started before one year and she visited multiple clinics for her persistent complaints with no clear diagnosis.

in_text_mentions: In March 2024, she began taking belimumab 600 mg IV while continuing on a daily dose of prednisone 5 mg. By April 2024, she was admitted to the hospital with nephrotic syndrome and leukopenia. Despite a kidney biopsy confirming Class II LN, the high level of proteinuria suggested that the disease might be more severe. The biopsy showed segmental sclerosis, mesangial expansion, and mild thickening of the basement membrane, with electron microscopy revealing extensive podocyte damage consistent with Class II LN (Figures 1 and 2). Table 1 shows laboratory findings on presentation.

A: PAS-stained kidney biopsy from an SLE patient showing class IV lupus nephritis with mesangial hypercellularity, GBM thickening, and subendothelial deposits (wire-loop lesions). B: Silver-stained kidney biopsy from an SLE patient showing class IV lupus nephritis with characteristic glomerular basement membrane and mesangial changes. C: Trichrome-stained kidney biopsy from an SLE patient showing class IV lupus nephritis with membranoproliferative pattern, subendothelial deposits, pseudo-thrombi, and interstitial fibroedema. panels.attribution_text: Simão et al. New-onset lupus nephritis and neuropsychiatric lupus following COVID-19 vaccination: A case report.. Clinical nephrology. Case studies 2026. doi:10.5414/cncs112003. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 1.
panels.figure_caption: Kidney biopsy fragment on optical microscopy (×200 magnification) using periodic acid–Schiff (A), silver (B), and trichrome (C) stains and immunofluorescence (×200 magnification). Glomeruli exhibit a membranoproliferative pattern of injury, characterized by mesangial expansion and hypercellularity (red arrows), along with thickening of the glomerular basement membrane (green arrows). Subendothelial deposits and pseudo-thrombi are more distinctly visualized on trichrome staining (black arrows). There is diffuse interstitial fibroedema involving the entire cortical compartment (blue arrows), accompanied by a mild mononuclear inflammatory infiltrate, as well as acute tubular necrosis throughout the cortical compartment. Immunofluorescence shows mesangial and capillary wall deposition of IgG++; IgA+; IgM+; C3+; C1q+, κ++, and λ++.
in_text_mentions: Renal biopsy confirmed class IV lupus nephritis (LN) (Figure 1). Electromyography revealed axonal sensory polyneuropathy. Brain MRI showed bilateral periventricular and subcortical white matter hyperintensities, interpreted as nonspecific but consistent with neuropsychiatric lupus in this context.

panels.figure_caption: Microscopic findings of the renal biopsy: Glomeruli are enlarged and hypercellular with moderate diffuse mesangial hypercellularity. Glomeruli also display segmental to global endocapillary proliferation by infiltrating mononuclear leukocytes and neutrophils. Also noted segmental membranoproliferative features with large sub-endothelial immune deposits with mild interstitial inflammation by lymphocytes, monocytes, neutrophils, and rare eosinophils involving 10% of the cortex.
in_text_mentions: ednisone due to suspicion of autoimmune process, but with no clinical improvement. Due to persistent symptoms and worsening anemia and kidney functions, he was evaluated by nephrology. The patient underwent a renal biopsy which showed diffuse endocapillary and focal membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis, consistent with class IV lupus nephritis, as shown in Figure 1. Immunofluorescence revealed a "full house" of immune staining and a granular global mesangial and glomerular capillary distribution, supporting a diagnosis of immune complex-mediated glomerulonephritis as shown in Figures 2, 3.

in_text_mentions: align with a typical drug-induced process. In January 2024, another flare prompted a second punch biopsy on the back, revealing a lymphocytic infiltrate with dermal mucin suggestive of CLE (Figures 3, 4). He began hydroxychloroquine 200 mg daily for two weeks, then 200 mg twice daily, with partial improvement in his skin lesions. Despite negative anti-double-stranded DNA, negative or fluctuating antinuclear antibody (ANA) titers, and mixed serologies such as positive anti-ribonucleoprotein (anti-RNP) and anti-smith (anti-Sm) in late 2023, there remained a concern for a lupus spectrum disease.

panels.rationale: Renal biopsy light microscopy image from a patient with hydralazine-induced lupus nephritis showing diffuse proliferative glomerulonephritis (Class IV lupus nephritis), a classic severe manifestation of SLE.
panels.attribution_text: Khan et al. Hydralazine-Induced Isolated Lupus Nephritis.. Ochsner journal 2020. doi:10.31486/toj.18.0128. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 1.
panels.figure_caption: Light microscopy shows diffuse proliferative glomerulonephritis (magnification ×40).
in_text_mentions: The patient was advised to discontinue hydralazine; however, his renal function did not improve upon drug discontinuation. His serum creatinine peaked at 5.2 mg/dL with a glomerular filtration rate <10 mL/min. Diagnostic kidney biopsy revealed diffuse proliferative glomerulonephritis (Figures 1 and 2). Immunofluorescence was consistent, with multiple immune deposits as seen in lupus nephritis (Figure 3). Based on these findings, the patient was diagnosed with hydralazine-induced lupus nephritis.

panels.rationale: Histology image of a skin biopsy from a patient with tumid lupus erythematosus (a cutaneous SLE variant), showing characteristic superficial and deep perivascular and periadnexal lymphocytic infiltrate with dermal mucin deposition and edema. [raw subtype: tle]
panels.attribution_text: Liu et al. Tumid Lupus Erythematosus: A Rare and Distinctive Variant of Cutaneous Lupus Erythematosus Masquerading as Urticarial Vasculitis.. Cureus 2020. doi:10.7759/cureus.8305. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 3.
panels.figure_caption: Hematoxylin and eosin stain of 4-mm punch biopsy (4x magnification) of lesion demonstrating superficial and deep perivascular and periadnexal lymphocytic infiltrate with dermal mucin deposition and edema.
in_text_mentions: els. Two 4-mm punch biopsies from lesions were taken from two different sites. They both demonstrated a superficial and deep perivascular and periadnexal lymphocytic infiltrate, dermal mucin, and edema (Figures 3-4). A colloidal iron immunohistochemical stain confirmed the excessive mucin deposition within the dermis (Figure 5). Given the clinical and histopathological correlation, a diagnosis of TLE was established. The patient was prescribed betamethasone dipropionate 0.05% spray and noted significant clinical improvement with near complete resolution at the follow-up visit, two weeks later.

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 4 panels (a, b, c, d). a: Human patient kidney biopsy H&E histology showing morphological features of diffuse proliferative lupus nephritis (class IV), a recognized subtype of SLE, as confirmed by the article's biopsy interpretation. b: Human patient kidney biopsy H&E histology showing a classic wire-loop lesion, a hallmark of active lupus nephritis, a subtype of SLE. c: Human patient kidney biopsy silver-stained histology showing a cellular crescent, a feature of active diffuse proliferative lupus nephritis (class IV), a subtype of SLE. d: Human patient kidney biopsy silver-stained histology showing fibrinoid necrosis of afferent arterioles, a complication of active lupus nephritis, a subtype of SLE.
panels.attribution_text: Kim et al. Eculizumab therapy on a patient with co-existent lupus nephritis and C3 mutation-related atypical haemolytic uremic syndrome: a case report.. BMC nephrology 2021. doi:10.1186/s12882-021-02293-2. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 2.
panels.figure_caption: Pathological findings of kidney biopsy. a Light microscopy, Haematoxylin and eosin staining (H&E). Lobular accentuation with panhypercellularity and multiple layers of capillary wall with focal segmental mesangiolysis (arrow). b Light microscopy, H&E. Glomerulus showing marked thickened capillary loop (wire loop lesion). c Light microscopy, silver staining. Cellular crescent in glomerulus. d Light microscopy, silver staining. Afferent arterioles affected by fibrinoid necrosis
in_text_mentions: On the 15th hospital day, ultrasound-guided percutaneous kidney biopsy was performed. Light microscopy of renal biopsy specimens has shown diffuse proliferative lupus nephritis, class IV-G (active) with mesangiolysis and arteriolar fibrin thrombi indicative of TMA (Fig. 2). Immunofluorescence staining has shown a “full-house” pattern (positive for IgG, IgA, IgM, C3, and C1q) in the mesangium and peripheral capillary wall. Based on these renal biopsy findings, a diagnosis of lupus nephritis with TMA was confirmed.

panels.rationale: Electron microscopy image of a renal biopsy showing electron-dense subendothelial deposits indicated by arrows, which is a classic histologic manifestation of lupus nephritis. The caption explicitly describes this finding and the article context supports lupus nephritis as the underlying disease process.

panels.figure_caption: Electron microscopy identified electron dense deposits in the subendothelial space (red long arrows), with associated formation of new basement membrane material internal to the deposits (black short arrow).
in_text_mentions: The final read of the biopsy demonstrated membranoproliferative glomerulopathy, immune complex‐mediated with rare cellular crescents, and foci of fibrinoid necrosis. The full house immunofluorescence staining suggests lupus nephritis as a possible etiology. Mild tubulitis and interstitial mononuclear inflammation meet the criteria for borderline/suspicious for acute T cell‐mediated rejection. (Figures 1, 2, 3, 4, 5).

findings.label: Dermal mucin deposition
findings.evidence: Mucin deposition is noted in the reticular dermis

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 4 panels (A, B, C, D). A: Low-power H&E of acral skin showing superficial and deep lymphocytic infiltrate and dermal mucin deposition, consistent with chilblain lupus erythematosus. B: Higher-power H&E demonstrating perivascular lymphocytic infiltrate in the reticular dermis without eosinophils, supporting a lupus erythematosus pattern. C: Alcian blue stain highlighting mucin deposition in the dermis, a characteristic histologic feature of lupus erythematosus. D: Direct immunofluorescence demonstrating granular IgM deposition at the dermoepidermal junction (lupus band test), a hallmark of cutaneous lupus erythematosus.
panels.attribution_text: Israr ul Haq et al. Palmar Cutaneous Erythematous Macules: A Case Report of an Atypical Presentation of Chilblain Lupus Erythematosus.. Cureus 2026. doi:10.7759/cureus.103293. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 3.
panels.figure_caption: A: Punch biopsy. A. The image displays acral skin with superficial and deep lymphocytic infiltrate, epidermal spongiosis is not seen (H&E stain, x50); B: Perivascular lymphocytic infiltrate is noted in the reticular dermis, no eosinophils are seen (H&E stain, x200); C: Mucin deposition is noted in the reticular dermis (AB 2.5 stain (Alcian Blue, pH 2.5), x400); D: Direct immunofluorescence showing granular positivity at the dermoepidermal junction (IgM x200).
in_text_mentions: Multiple investigations were undertaken to assess the underlying etiology of this rash. Punch biopsy of the eruption on the hands was obtained, which showed superficial and deep perivascular lymphocytic infiltrate with dermal mucin (Figures 3A-3C). There was no significant epidermal spongiosis, eosinophilic infiltrate, or definitive interface dermatitis. Also, direct immunofluorescence studies showed granular IgM and IgG deposition at the dermoepidermal junction (Figure 3D).

in_text_mentions: els. Two 4-mm punch biopsies from lesions were taken from two different sites. They both demonstrated a superficial and deep perivascular and periadnexal lymphocytic infiltrate, dermal mucin, and edema (Figures 3-4). A colloidal iron immunohistochemical stain confirmed the excessive mucin deposition within the dermis (Figure 5). Given the clinical and histopathological correlation, a diagnosis of TLE was established. The patient was prescribed betamethasone dipropionate 0.05% spray and noted significant clinical improvement with near complete resolution at the follow-up visit, two weeks later.

findings.label: Non-scarring alopecia
findings.evidence: Dermoscopy shows non-scarring alopecia with intact hair follicles and no epidermal changes.

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 4 panels (A, B, C, D). A: Clinical photograph of a human scalp lesion explicitly described as an annular erythematous plaque associated with non-scarring alopecia, supporting tumid lupus erythematosus as a lupus manifestation. B: Clinical photograph of a temporal scalp lesion explicitly described as an erythematous plaque in a case of tumid lupus erythematosus, associated with non-scarring alopecia. C: Clinical photograph of an occipital scalp plaque explicitly described in the caption and article text as part of the tumid lupus presentation with non-scarring alopecia and hair miniaturization. D: Dermoscopic image from the captioned tumid lupus lesion showing arborizing vessels over erythema and non-scarring alopecia with preserved follicles, supporting lupus-associated inflammatory alopecia.
panels.attribution_text: Alharbe et al. An Uncommon Presentation of Tumid Lupus Erythematosus Manifesting As Annular, Non-scarring Alopecia on the Scalp.. Cureus 2025. doi:10.7759/cureus.77085. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 1.
panels.figure_caption: A, B, and C showing three annular erythematous plaques over the scalp. D shows a dermoscopic view of the lesion A: The arrow highlights an annular erythematous plaque over the temporoparietal side of the scalp. B: The arrow highlights an erythematous plaque over the temporal side of the scalp. C: The arrow highlights an erythematous plaque over the occipital side of the scalp. D: Dermoscopy shows arborizing blood vessels (indicated by the arrow) and non-scarring alopecia without epidermal changes. Intact hair follicles, free of obstruction or keratinous plugging, can be seen. Although hair follicles appear intact in the affected regions, the alopecia is due to inflammation associated with TLE, which does not lead to permanent follicular damage.
in_text_mentions: On physical examination, three non-scaly, erythematous, and edematous annular plaques were observed, involving the occipital area and bilateral temporal regions of the scalp. These plaques were associated with non-scarring alopecia and hair miniaturization over the frontal and vertex areas (Figure 1A, 1B, 1C). Dermoscopic examination showed arborizing blood vessels overlying a background of erythema, with intact hair follicles free of obstruction or keratinous plugging. The interfollicular spaces appeared normal, without scaling, ulceration, or atrophy (Figure 1D).

panels.figure_caption: Clinical, dermoscopic, and histopathologic images at current presentation. A1-A3, Clinical images of the lower leg from the posterior view at age 8 years, demonstrating dark red and brown linear atrophic plaques with mild hyperkeratosis and central atrophy, featuring well-defined borders along Blaschko’s lines on the medial right lower extremity. B, Dermoscopy of chronic lesions demonstrates skin atrophy and whitening (white arrow), white structureless areas (black arrow), and an irregular distribution of fine curved linear (green arrow), arborizing (yellow arrow), and atypical dilated (blue arrow) vessels. Follicular ostia are absent, and the “rosette sign” (4 white points in a cloverleaf-like pattern, red arrow) is observed. C, Dermoscopy of new lesions shows central erythema with sparse yellow-white scales (black arrow), follicular plugging (green arrow), perifollicular white halos (blue arrow), multicyclic erythema (white arrow), and irregular pigmentation (yellow arrow). D, Histopathology of the right ankle reveals hyperkeratosis and an atrophic epidermis. Interface dermatitis, liquefactive degeneration of the basal cell layer, a few melanophagocytes in the superficial dermis, and perivascular and periadnexal lymphocytic inflammatory infiltrate in the superficial and deep dermis are present (original magnification ×40). E, PAS staining highlights prominent basement membrane thickening (original magnification ×40). F, Mucin staining reveals interstitial mucin deposition within the dermis (original magnification ×40). G, Immunohistochemical analysis for CD123 demonstrates plasmacytoid dendritic cells (PDCs) aggregating in clusters within perivascular and periadnexal regions (original magnification ×40).
in_text_mentions: Current physical examination revealed dark red and brown linear atrophic plaques with mild hyperkeratosis and central atrophy (Fig 2, A). Histopathologically, this sign corresponds to follicular plugging and infundibular hyperkeratosis (Fig 2, B).3 In the context of linear inflammatory lesions, this presence serves as a robust diagnostic clue favoring discoid-type lupus erythematosus over other blaschkoid dermatoses. High levels of anti-Ro and aPL [4,37] and positivity for cryoglobulins [38] are associated with a major risk of developing cutaneous lupus vasculitis. High levels of anti-Ro and aPL [4,37] and positivity for cryoglobulins [38] are associated with a major risk of developing cutaneous lupus vasculitis. panels.attribution_text: Uva et al. Cutaneous manifestations of systemic lupus erythematosus.. Autoimmune diseases 2012. doi:10.1155/2012/834291. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 8.
panels.figure_caption: Vasculitis.
in_text_mentions: Cutaneous vasculitis is presented in a multivariety of morphological lesions such as punctuate lesions, palpable purpura, urticaria, ulcers, papules, erythematosus plaques or macules, and erythema with necrosis that may be self-limiting or relapsing (Figure 8). C: Caption identifies DLE Case 6 with deeply infiltrated discoid plaques on face; image shows erythematous infiltrated papules/plaques on cheek. D: Caption identifies TEN-like (ACLE) lupus early presentation; image shows diffuse erythema with widespread eruption on chest; no vocabulary key for TEN-like detachment so captured as proposed findings. E: Caption identifies TEN-like (ACLE) lupus late presentation with progression of clinical picture; image shows extensive erythema with peeling on back; no vocabulary key so captured as proposed findings.

panels.rationale: Single DIF image from photo-exposed lesional skin in case of Rowell syndrome-like flare of cutaneous lupus erythematosus. Caption and in-text describe positive lupus band at DEJ (IgA, IgM, C3). Real human-patient immunofluorescence showing lupus_band manifestation of sle. Subtype not specified for this panel, so subtype null.

panels.figure_caption: Direct immunofluorescence on a biopsy from a lesion on photo exposed skin showing a granular band of immuno-reactant deposition along the dermal-epidermal junction.
in_text_mentions: Direct immunofluorescence revealed the presence of a positive lupus band of immune reactants at the DEJ in both lesional (IgA, IgM, complement C3) and clinically uninvolved non-exposed skin (IgM) (Figure 4). Dust-like epidermal fluorescence was not found in any of the biopsy specimens.

in_text_mentions: On admission, echocardiography demonstrated a large, free-flowing pericardial effusion circumferential to the heart, measuring up to 2.9 cm, with mild right atrial and right ventricular collapse concerning for early tamponade physiology, as well as a left-sided pleural effusion (Figure 1). Chest X-ray confirmed cardiomegaly and a small-to-moderate left pleural effusion with left basilar atelectasis (Figure 2).

panels.figure_caption: Initial presentation of the patient’s scalp with an area of alopecia

in_text_mentions: With the 24-hour urinary protein level elevated at 650 mg/day, suspicion of LN arose, prompting a renal biopsy for further evaluation. Her sputum examination was done, cultures showed no growth or organism, and her GeneXpert did not detect mycobacterium tuberculosis.

findings.label: Interface dermatitis
findings.evidence: focal full-thickness epidermal necrosis with interface dermatitis

panels.rationale: Single H&E skin biopsy from abdomen/trunk with interface dermatitis and full-thickness epidermal necrosis. In-text interpretation explicitly attributes to interface dermatitis in setting of ACLE TEN-like variant/RS, correlating with clinical/serological SLE findings. Title 'TEN-Like Cutaneous Lupus' is about lupus (configured disease), not true drug-induced SJS/TEN, so tagged as sle acle.
panels.attribution_text: Bakhsh et al. Overlap of Toxic Epidermal Necrolysis (TEN)-Like Cutaneous Lupus and Rowell Syndrome in Systemic Lupus Erythematosus: A Case-Based Review.. Cureus 2025. doi:10.7759/cureus.95603. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 5.
panels.figure_caption: Skin biopsy of the patient with diffuse erythema of the abdomen and trunk showing focal full-thickness epidermal necrosis with interface dermatitis. Key histopathological features, including (1) basal cell vacuolar degeneration, (2) lymphocytic infiltrate at the dermo-epidermal junction, and (3) epidermal necrosis, are marked in the image for clarity. Epidermal necrosis appears as shrunken, eosinophilic (pink-staining) keratinocytes with pyknotic nuclei (condensed, dark nuclei) and a loss of cellular detail, indicating cell death.
in_text_mentions: is. Areas of subepidermal cleft formation are identified. At the dermo-epidermal junction, there is a band-like lymphocytic infiltrate, with associated papillary dermal edema and perivascular lymphocytic aggregates, occasionally admixed with eosinophils. Importantly, there is no evidence of leukocytoclasia, microabscess formation, or festooning of dermal papillae (Figure 5). The interpretation concluded that the histopathological features are most consistent with interface dermatitis in the setting of ACLE (TEN-like variant/RS), correlating with the clinical and serological findings (Table 2).
